Only on the fourth day are the lights made, and their stated work is the same: to divide the day from the night, to give light on the earth, and to divide the light from the darkness. Nothing earlier in Genesis uses the phrase “sons of God”, and the passage does not explain it. original.summary: Melchizedek appears for three verses as king of Salem and priest of the most high God, blesses Abram and receives a tenth, and is not mentioned again in Genesis. His people, his descent and how he came to be a priest are not stated.

Melchizedek is introduced without parents, people or history; he is a king of a city in the land where Abram is a stranger, and he is priest of the God whom Abram in verse 22 names as the Lord. Abram accepts his blessing and a tenth is given. The passage does not say how a king of Salem came to serve that God, who made him a priest, or what became of him.

title: Is the angel of the Lord a messenger, or the Lord himself?

original.summary: In Genesis the angel of the Lord speaks in the first person as God: “I will multiply thy seed”, “thou hast not withheld thy son … from me”, “I am the God of Bethel”. Hagar names “the Lord that spake unto her”. The passages do not say whether the angel is someone other than God or God himself appearing.
original.reasoning: The narrator calls the speaker “the angel of the Lord” or “the angel of God”. The speaker then says things in the first person that belong to God: he will multiply Hagar’s seed; Abraham has not withheld his son “from me”; “I am the God of Bethel”. In the same speeches he also speaks of God as another: “the Lord hath heard thy affliction” (16:11), “thou fearest God” (22:12). Hagar’s response is to name “the Lord that spake unto her”. At 22:16 the words are marked as a message, “saith the Lord”; at 16:10 and 31:13 there is no such mark. The passages do not say whether the angel is a being sent by God who speaks God’s words, or God appearing.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have taken the angel as a messenger who speaks his sender’s words in the first person, as an appearance of God himself, or as a distinct divine person. Each is an interpretation; the passages state none of them, and this record asserts none. The same alternation is found outside Genesis: at the bush the angel of the Lord appears and God calls (Exodus 3:2, 3:4), and Manoah, knowing he had seen an angel of the Lord, says they have seen God (Judges 13:21–22). In Zechariah 1:12 the angel of the Lord addresses the Lord of hosts as another. These show the question recurs; they do not settle it for Genesis. title: Who were the three men at Mamre, and was the Lord one of them?

original.summary: The Lord appears to Abraham; Abraham looks up and sees three men. Later “the men” leave for Sodom while Abraham still stands before the Lord, and two angels arrive at Sodom. The passage does not say how the Lord and the three men are related, or why three become two.

Through the meal and the promise the speaker changes without comment: “they said” (18:9), “he said” (18:10), “the Lord said” (18:13). In verse 22 “the men” go toward Sodom while Abraham still stands before the Lord, and in 19:1 two angels reach Sodom, who say the Lord has sent them. The passage does not say whether the Lord was one of the three, whether all three were his messengers, or what became of the third between Mamre and Sodom.

title: 430 years in Egypt, yet Kohath, Amram and Moses span at most 350

original.summary: Kohath is named among those who came into Egypt. He lived 133 years, his son Amram 137, and Amram’s son Moses was 80 at the exodus. Those three figures add up to 350 years at the very most, yet Exodus says Israel dwelt in Egypt 430 years.
original.reasoning: Kohath is listed among those who came into Egypt, so he was already born when the 430 years began. Suppose Amram was born in the last year of Kohath’s 133 years, and Moses in the last year of Amram’s 137. Moses was 80 when he spoke to Pharaoh. 133 + 137 + 80 = 350. title: Silver from 603,550 men numbered — a month before the numbering that gives that total

original.summary: The silver for the sockets of the tabernacle came from 603,550 men who were numbered, and the tabernacle was reared on the first day of the first month of the second year. The numbering that yields 603,550 is commanded on the first day of the second month of that year.
original.reasoning: The sockets were cast from the silver of those numbered, so that numbering was complete before the tabernacle was reared on the first day of the first month. The numbering in Numbers is commanded a month later, on the first day of the second month, and its total is the same figure to the last man: 603,550. Either one numbering is placed at two different times, or two numberings a month or more apart gave an identical total.
original.scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek have the same total as the KJV in both books. In Brenton’s Greek the chapters on the making of the tabernacle are in a different order, and KJV 38:26 is printed as 39:3. The count in Numbers leaves out the Levites (Numbers 1:47), and Exodus 38 does not say whether its count does. No claim is made about the actual number of the people. title: Which kings of Egypt were the Pharaohs of the oppression and the exodus?

original.summary: Exodus tells of a new king who knew not Joseph, of his death, and of the Pharaoh whom Moses faced, and names none of them. Later books name kings of Egypt. Which king oppressed Israel, and which let them go, is not stated.
original.reasoning: The story turns on at least two kings: the one who began the oppression and died, and the one who refused Moses and then let Israel go. Each is called only “the king of Egypt” or “Pharaoh”. Who they were decides when the events are placed and against which Egyptian records they can be compared, so the gap is a material one. It is not that the books never name Egyptian kings: Shishak, Pharaohnechoh and Pharaohhophra are named in Kings and Jeremiah.

title: The “Red sea” — the Hebrew says “sea of suph”, and has no word for red

original.summary: Where the KJV has “the Red sea”, the Hebrew has “sea of suph”. The KJV renders the same word suph as “flags” at Exodus 2:3 and “weeds” at Jonah 2:5. The Hebrew has no word for “red” in these verses. Brenton’s Greek has “Red sea”, as the KJV does.
original.reasoning: The Hebrew name of the sea is made of two words: “sea” and suph. Suph is a word for water plants: the KJV itself has “flags” for it where the infant Moses is laid by the river, and “weeds” where Jonah speaks of the deep. So the Hebrew name says “sea of reeds” or “sea of weeds”. “Red” is a different meaning, and no Hebrew word for red stands in any of these verses. The KJV’s “Red sea” matches the Greek name, not the Hebrew one.

title: “The morrow after the sabbath”: which sabbath starts the count of fifty days?

original.summary: The sheaf of firstfruits is waved “on the morrow after the sabbath”, and fifty days are counted from that day to the next feast. The named feasts discussed in the notes have stated month dates, while this count depends on “the sabbath”. It does not say which sabbath is meant, so the date of the sheaf, and of the feast fifty days later, is left open.
original.reasoning: Passover, unleavened bread, trumpets, atonement and tabernacles are each given a day of a month in this chapter. The sheaf and the feast fifty days after it are not: they hang on “the sabbath”. Nothing in 23:9–16 says whether this is the weekly sabbath that falls in the week of unleavened bread, the first day of that feast, its seventh day, or the first weekly sabbath after harvest begins. Each choice gives a different day for the sheaf, and so a different day for the feast that follows.

title: Seven sevens make forty-nine years; the jubile is the fiftieth. Where does the fiftieth year stand in the count?

original.summary: Every seventh year the land is not sown. Seven such sevens are forty-nine years, and then the fiftieth year is hallowed and not sown either. The chapter does not say whether the fiftieth year stands outside the sevens or is counted as the first year of the next seven. Under either reading that keeps it distinct from the forty-ninth, the two consecutive years are unsown.
original.reasoning: The forty-ninth year is a seventh year, so it is not sown. The fiftieth is the jubile and is not sown. If the fiftieth is a distinct year after the forty-ninth, two years pass without sowing whether the next seven starts at year fifty or year fifty-one; the quoted instructions do not specify that starting point. The promise in 25:20–22 is given for “the seventh year”: the sixth year yields “for three years”, sowing resumes in “the eighth year”, and old store lasts “until the ninth”. The quoted provision does not explicitly explain how the seventh-year sowing timetable applies at the jubile. The length of the cycle, forty-nine years or fifty, depends on the answer, and land prices and the release of servants in the same chapter are reckoned by years to the jubile.

title: Who was the Ethiopian woman Moses had married, and what was the complaint about her?

original.summary: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses “because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married”. The woman is not named, the passage does not say when Moses married her, and it does not say what the objection was. The next verse turns to a different matter and she is not mentioned again in the chapter.
original.reasoning: The marriage is given as the occasion of the whole episode, which ends with Miriam leprous and shut out of the camp. Yet the reader is not told who the woman is. The only wife of Moses named in the passages checked is Zipporah, daughter of the priest of Midian. Whether the woman of Numbers 12:1 is Zipporah under another description or a second wife changes what Miriam and Aaron are objecting to, and the passage gives the objection no words: what they are reported as saying is about prophecy.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that she is Zipporah, described by a name that Habakkuk 3:7 sets beside Midian (“Cushan”); that she is a second wife from the land the KJV calls Ethiopia, married after or beside Zipporah; that the complaint was about her people, or about the marriage itself, or was a pretext for the challenge of verse 2. original.summary: Numbers cites a written source by name, “the book of the wars of the Lord”, to support a statement about the border at Arnon. No book of that name is among the books of the KJV, the passage does not say who wrote it or when, and the words quoted from it break off without a finished sentence.

The passage gives a title and a fragment and nothing else: not the author, not the date, not what else the book held. original.summary: From the Midianite captives, one person in five hundred of the soldiers’ half is levied as tribute and given to Eleazar the priest as a heave offering: thirty-two persons. title: Who buried Moses?

original.summary: Deuteronomy says of Moses “he buried him” and that no man knows the grave. The verse does not name the one who buried him. Jude speaks of a dispute between Michael and the devil “about the body of Moses” and does not say what the dispute was or who buried the body.
original.reasoning: The burial of Moses is told in one clause with an unnamed subject, and the verse adds that the place is unknown. Who carried out the burial bears on how the unknown grave is to be understood: a burial by the people who then mourned thirty days might suggest a known grave, while a burial by God is one proposed explanation for its being unknown. Neither kind of burier by itself establishes whether the location would remain known. The verse gives the valley and its neighbourhood and still says no man knows the sepulchre.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that “he” is the Lord, the last one named in verse 5; that the singular verb has an indefinite subject, “one buried him”, which is how the plural of Brenton’s Greek can be taken; that Moses was buried by an angel, a reading that draws on Jude 1:9. Jude does not say that Michael buried Moses. title: The sun, moon and stars “divided unto all nations” — divided to them for what?

original.summary: Israel is warned not to worship the sun, moon and stars, “which the Lord thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven”. The verse does not say for what purpose they were divided to the nations. The next verse sets Israel apart: “But the Lord hath taken you”.
original.reasoning: The clause stands inside a warning against worshipping the heavenly bodies, and gives as a fact about them that God divided them to all nations. What was given to the nations — the use of their light, or the bodies as what those nations serve — changes what the passage says about the worship of other peoples. The same Hebrew verb is used at 29:26 (WLC 29:25) of gods “whom he had not given unto them”, said of Israel.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that the heavenly bodies were given to every nation alike for light and for marking time, as Genesis 1:17 says they were set “to give light upon the earth”, so that the clause is a reason not to worship what serves everyone; that they were allotted to the other nations as what those nations worship, while Israel was taken as the Lord’s own people (4:20), which is how the shared verb at 29:26 can be taken. The second reading does not by itself mean that such worship is approved. Check made: Deuteronomy 4:15–20, 17:2–5 and 29:24–28 were read in the KJV, and the Hebrew and Greek of the clauses quoted were compared; no other passage was searched, so a statement of the purpose elsewhere is not excluded. title: Moses blesses “the children of Israel” tribe by tribe — why is Simeon not named?

original.summary: Deuteronomy 33 is introduced as the blessing with which Moses blessed the children of Israel, and it names the tribes one after another. Simeon is not named in the chapter. The chapter gives no reason, though Simeon is named among the tribes six chapters earlier.
original.reasoning: The heading says the blessing is of the children of Israel, and the chapter then speaks of Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph with Ephraim and Manasseh, Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali and Asher. One of the tribes numbered in the wilderness and placed on mount Gerizim in chapter 27 has no saying. Whether that is a judgement on the tribe, a statement about its standing at the time, or an accident of the text changes how the chapter is read, and the chapter does not say.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the chapter states: that Simeon is passed over because of what Jacob says of Simeon and Levi in Genesis 49:5–7, though Levi is blessed here; that Simeon is counted within Judah, in whose land the tribe later has its inheritance (Joshua 19:1); that the tribe had become small, as the two numberings quoted may suggest; that a saying for Simeon has dropped out of the text. title: Who is the “captain of the host of the Lord” that Joshua meets by Jericho?

original.summary: By Jericho Joshua sees “a man” with a drawn sword who calls himself “captain of the host of the Lord”. Joshua falls on his face and is told to take off his shoe because the place is holy. The passage does not say who or what this figure is, and his command about the holy ground does not explicitly identify him.
original.reasoning: The figure is first called “a man”, then gives himself a title found in the KJV only in these two verses, and Joshua answers by falling on his face and calling him “my Lord”. Whether Joshua is meeting a human officer, an angel or God bears on what Joshua’s act is and on who speaks next: the three verses give no message from the captain beyond the command about the shoe, and the next words of instruction are introduced with “And the Lord said unto Joshua” after a verse about Jericho being shut up.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that the captain is an angel who commands the heavenly armies; that he is the Lord appearing in the form of a man, so that Joshua 6:2 continues the same meeting, a reading that points to the words about holy ground said to Moses at Exodus 3:5; that he is Christ before his birth, a reading held by some Christian interpreters. Limits on each: the Hebrew verb the KJV renders “did worship” here is the verb it renders “bowed himself” at Genesis 23:7, where it is done to men, so the verb alone does not show that the one bowed to is God, and a shared verb does not settle context; Revelation 22:8–9 has an angel refuse worship, which is quoted as a text used in this debate and not as an answer about Joshua; the passage does not say that the speaker of 6:2 is the captain. title: Rahab’s house was “upon the town wall” — how were the spies sent into it after “the wall fell down flat”?

original.summary: Rahab’s house is said to be upon the wall of Jericho, and her family is to be kept safe by staying inside it. The account then says the wall “fell down flat”, and the narrative next reports Joshua’s instruction and the spies going in to bring the family out. The verses compared do not say how the house was still there to be entered.
original.reasoning: The agreement with Rahab depends on the house: her family must be inside it, and the window in the wall is to be marked. The fall of the wall is then told without any exception, and the next thing said of the house is Joshua’s reported instruction and the spies going in and bringing the family out. The KJV “had said” does not fix the instruction itself as later than the collapse. Whether the house stood, and so whether the whole wall fell or a part of it, changes how “the wall fell down flat” is to be read, and the verses compared do not say.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses state: that the stretch of wall with her house was left standing; that the wall fell where the people stood and went up “every man straight before him”, and not on every side; that the house was built against the side of the wall, as the Hebrew wording quoted can be taken, and was not brought down with it; that the account is brief and passes over how the family came through. title: “Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God” — which words, and in which book?

original.summary: After the covenant at Shechem, Joshua is said to have written “these words in the book of the law of God”. The verse does not say which words he wrote, or whether the book is the book of the law that Moses wrote and had placed beside the ark, which the book of Joshua elsewhere calls “the book of the law of Moses”.
original.reasoning: Deuteronomy says Moses wrote the words of the law in a book “until they were finished” and had it put beside the ark. Joshua then writes in a book with a like name. If it is the same book, Joshua’s writing was added to that book after Moses, without establishing an addition to the substantive law; if it is another book, the passage speaks of a second writing that it does not describe. What “these words” covers — the covenant of that day, its statute and ordinance, or a longer account — is not said either, and it bears on what the passage claims about who wrote what.

Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that Joshua added a record of the Shechem covenant to the book Moses wrote; that “the book of the law of God” is a separate writing kept at the sanctuary; that “these words” are the statute and ordinance of verse 25 only; that the phrase points to the writing of the book of Joshua or of part of it. title: Judges opens “after the death of Joshua”, then tells of Joshua sending the people away and dying — in what order did these things happen?

original.summary: The first verse of Judges dates what follows “after the death of Joshua”. A chapter later Joshua lets the people go and his death is reported. One event of chapter 1, the taking of Kirjathsepher by Othniel, is also told in Joshua 15 in almost the same words. The verses compared do not say which of these events came before Joshua’s death and which after.
original.reasoning: The opening words give a time for what follows, and the question Israel asks in the same verse leads into the campaigns of chapter 1. Yet 2:6–8 has Joshua alive, dismissing the people, and then dying, in words close to Joshua 24:28–29; and the taking of Kirjathsepher with the gift of Achsah stands both here and in Joshua 15:15–17, where it follows a grant to Caleb made “according to the commandment of the Lord to Joshua”. The order matters for reading chapter 1: it decides whether those campaigns are new wars fought after Joshua or a second telling of wars from his time, and so how they sit beside the conquest summaries in Joshua.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Judges 1:1 is a heading for the book and chapter 1 gathers events of different times, some from Joshua’s lifetime; that everything in chapter 1 happened after Joshua’s death and Joshua 15:15–17 tells in advance of a later event; that Judges 2:6–10 goes back in time and takes up the end of the book of Joshua before the story moves on. title: What was the ephod Gideon made of the gold, and what did Israel do when it “went thither a whoring after it”?

original.summary: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the spoil, makes “an ephod thereof” and puts it in his city, and all Israel goes “a whoring after it”. In the other verses compared an ephod is a thing a priest wears or brings. The passage does not say what Gideon’s ephod was, what it was for, or what the people did with it.
original.reasoning: In the verses compared outside Judges an ephod is listed among garments, is worn (“girded with a linen ephod”), or is brought by a priest when David wants to enquire. Gideon’s is made from the collected gold earrings, whose total weight is given as seventeen hundred shekels; the amount used in the ephod is not specified. It is “put” in a town, and draws “all Israel”. The passage gives the result, a snare to Gideon and his house, without saying what the object was or what the people did. That bears on what Gideon is being charged with, straight after he has said “the Lord shall rule over you”: making an idol, or setting up a means of enquiry or of priestly service away from the sanctuary.

title: What was the “evil spirit” God sent between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and how did it work?

original.summary: After three years of Abimelech’s rule “God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem”, and the men of Shechem turn on him. The next verse gives the purpose: the blood of Gideon’s sons is to come upon both. The passage does not say what the evil spirit was or how it brought the treachery about.

title: Jephthah “did with her according to his vow” — what was done to his daughter?

original.summary: Jephthah vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him “shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering”. His only child comes out. After two months she returns and he “did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man”. Verse 39 reports fulfillment by reference to the vow, without separately describing the act.
original.reasoning: The vow names a burnt offering, and the fulfilment is told in seven English words that point back to the vow without repeating it. What the passage dwells on instead is her virginity: she asks two months to bewail it, and the report of the fulfilment is followed at once by “and she knew no man”. The reference back to a vow naming a burnt offering provides textual support for the reading that Jephthah sacrificed his daughter. Other readings depend on interpreting the vow or its fulfillment differently. title: Naomi “selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech's” — how did the land come to be hers to sell?

original.summary: Boaz tells the nearer kinsman that Naomi “selleth a parcel of land” that was Elimelech’s, and afterwards says he has bought all that was Elimelech’s, Chilion’s and Mahlon’s “of the hand of Naomi”. The order of inheritance given in Numbers 27:8–11 names a son, a daughter, brethren, the father’s brethren and the nearest kinsman. The verses compared do not say how the land came into Naomi’s hand, or what exactly she was selling.
original.reasoning: The sale is the business Boaz brings to the gate: it is what he puts to the nearer kinsman, and what he afterwards says he has bought. Elimelech and both his sons are dead (1:3, 1:5), and the land is spoken of as Elimelech’s, Chilion’s and Mahlon’s, yet it passes “of the hand of Naomi”. The order of inheritance quoted from Numbers passes a dead man’s inheritance to a son, a daughter, his brethren, his father’s brethren and then his nearest kinsman; those four verses do not name his widow. How Naomi held the land decides what the redeemer was acquiring from her — the field itself, the use of it, or a right over land already in another’s hands — and bears on why Ruth is joined to the purchase at 4:5.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, whose legal basis or historical application the verses quoted do not settle: that a widow kept her husband’s land for her lifetime, or until an heir was raised, by a custom not written in the laws quoted; that the land had passed out of the family’s hands when they went to Moab and what Naomi offers is the right to redeem it, the case Leviticus 25:25 speaks of; that the land was assigned to Naomi, as the Greek quoted says it “has been given” to her. Limits: Numbers 27:8–11 is given in answer to a case about daughters and does not say that its order is the only way land could be held, so its not naming a widow is not a statement that a widow could hold nothing; 2 Kings 8:3 and 8:6 speak of a woman’s house and land as “hers” and are quoted to show that wording, and they do not say how she held them or that her case was like Naomi’s; the Hebrew verb at 4:3 is a form usually rendered as past and can also state an act done in the speaking, and the verses quoted do not say whether a sale had already been made; the Greek “has been given” differs from the KJV’s “selleth” and that difference is not examined here. title: By what law or custom did redeeming Elimelech’s field carry the duty “to raise up the name of the dead” through Ruth?

original.summary: The nearer kinsman agrees to redeem the field. Boaz then joins Ruth, “the wife of the dead”, to the purchase, “to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance”, and the kinsman withdraws. The law of redemption quoted from Leviticus speaks of land, and the law quoted from Deuteronomy speaks of a husband’s brother. The verses compared do not say what joined the two duties in a kinsman who is not called the dead man’s brother.
original.reasoning: The story turns on this link. The nearer kinsman says “I will redeem it” while only the field is named (4:4), and says “I cannot redeem it” once Ruth and the name of the dead are joined to it (4:5–6). Leviticus 25:25 speaks of a kinsman redeeming what was sold, and that verse says nothing of a widow. Deuteronomy 25:5–7 speaks of “brethren” who “dwell together” and of the “husband's brother” taking the widow. Boaz is called a kinsman of Naomi’s husband, “of the family of Elimelech” (2:1), and calls Elimelech “our brother” (4:3); the verses quoted do not call Boaz or the nearer kinsman a brother of Mahlon. The passage does not state the rule under which a redeemer of the land took on the dead man’s name, or whether the nearer kinsman was bound by it or free to decline.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. title: Boaz took Ruth “to raise up the name of the dead”, and “Boaz begat Obed” — how was the dead man’s name raised, and was the child also counted legally in his house?

original.summary: Boaz says he takes Ruth “to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off”. When the child is born the women say, “There is a son born to Naomi”, and the list that closes the book says “Boaz begat Obed”. The verses compared give Obed as the son of Boaz and do not name Mahlon or Elimelech in the line; they do not say how the name of the dead was raised up.
original.reasoning: The purpose is stated twice, at 4:5 and 4:10, and it is the ground Boaz gives for the marriage before the witnesses. Deuteronomy 25:6 says of the case it covers that the firstborn “shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead”. Yet after 4:10 the book does not name Mahlon again: the women speak of a son born to Naomi, and the list of 4:18–22 runs from Salmon to Boaz to Obed. The same descent stands in 1 Chronicles 2:12, Matthew 1:5 and Luke 3:32. The book ends on David (4:17, 4:22), and the genealogies explicitly trace David’s descent through Boaz and Obed. The remaining question concerns whether any separate legal or inheritance reckoning preserved the dead man’s name; the verses quoted do not specify that arrangement.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. title: “Bring me up Samuel” — by what means did Samuel come up at Endor, and why did the woman cry out?

original.summary: The Lord does not answer Saul “by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets”. Saul then asks a woman “that hath a familiar spirit” to bring up Samuel, who is dead. The next sentence says the woman “saw Samuel” and “cried with a loud voice”, and the passage goes on to give words of Samuel that speak in the name of the Lord. The verses compared do not say what the woman did, by whose act Samuel came up, or why she cried out.
original.reasoning: The passage sets two things side by side. The laws quoted forbid consulting one “that hath a familiar spirit”, and 28:6 says the Lord would not answer Saul by the three means it names. Yet from 28:12 the narrative itself uses the name Samuel for what the woman sees and for the speaker (“the woman saw Samuel”, “Samuel said to Saul”), and the words spoken name the Lord and say what will happen the next day. Between the request at 28:11 and the sight at 28:12 no act of the woman is told. So the verses quoted leave unstated whether Samuel came up through the woman’s practice, apart from it, or in some other way, and they give no reason for her cry or for how she then knew her visitor was Saul. Which of these is taken decides how the passage bears on the laws quoted and on the statement that the Lord did not answer.

title: What became of Shiloh, and of the house of the Lord there, after “the ark of God was taken”?

original.summary: In 1 Samuel 1–4 the yearly worship, Eli’s priesthood and the ark are at Shiloh. The ark is taken in battle and a runner brings the news to Shiloh. The compared passages do not narrate what happened to the sanctuary at Shiloh: the returned ark goes to Kirjathjearim, and priests with the shewbread are later described at Nob. Jeremiah says “see what I did to it” and a psalm says God “forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh”. The verses compared do not say what was done to Shiloh, when, or by whom.
original.reasoning: Shiloh is where the tabernacle was set up (Joshua 18:1) and where the first chapters of 1 Samuel place the sacrifices, the priests and the ark. The cited scene at Shiloh reports the arrival of news that the ark was taken (4:12 and the verses after it). When the ark comes back it is not brought to Shiloh, and priests with the shewbread are later at Nob. Jeremiah points to Shiloh as a place where something was done that his hearers could go and see, and makes it the pattern for what will be done to the house in Jerusalem; Psalm 78 says God forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh. None of the verses compared narrates that event. What it was, and whether it followed the battle of 1 Samuel 4 or came later, bears on how the later priestly setting at Nob, the separate resting place of the ark and Jeremiah’s warning are read; these verses do not directly narrate a move of the priesthood from Shiloh to Nob.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the Philistines destroyed Shiloh after the battle; that the place was left by the priests without being destroyed, and that what Jeremiah speaks of happened at a later time; that the forsaking in Psalm 78 is the loss of the ark and nothing more. title: “Michal took an image, and laid it in the bed” — what was it, and how did it come to be in David's house?

original.summary: To cover David’s escape Michal puts “an image” in his bed, and Saul’s messengers find it there. The Hebrew word is the one the KJV prints as “teraphim” in Judges, renders “images” where Rachel steals her father’s and Laban calls them “my gods”, and renders “idolatry” in Samuel’s rebuke of Saul. The verses compared do not say what the object was, whose it was, or what it was kept for.
original.reasoning: The object is the means of the escape, and the Hebrew gives it the definite article: “the teraphim”. The article alone does not establish its ownership or prior use in the household. In the other verses quoted the same Hebrew word names things a man calls “my gods” (Genesis 31:30), things made with an ephod for “an house of gods” (Judges 17:5), things Josiah put away with the idols (2 Kings 23:24), and the thing to which Samuel likens Saul’s stubbornness (1 Samuel 15:23). Here it lies in David’s bed, and the verses quoted pass no remark on it. What it was and whose it was decides whether the passage shows an object of worship kept in David’s house, something of Michal’s own, or a thing with another use.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that it was a household figure of the kind Laban calls his gods; that it belonged to Michal and not to David; that it was a figure kept for some use other than worship; that it was large enough to pass for a man in a bed. Limits: a shared Hebrew word does not show that the object in David’s house was the same kind of thing as Laban’s or Micah’s, or that it was used as theirs were; the Hebrew word is plural in form in every verse quoted, and the KJV renders it “an image” here and “images” in Genesis, so its form does not settle whether one object or several is meant; the verses quoted do not say the object had a human shape or size — they say it was laid in the bed and covered, and that Michal said “He is sick”; Rachel sits upon hers (Genesis 31:34), which says something of the size of those and nothing of this one; the passage does not say David knew of the object, and it records no word of blame or of approval; no finding of a broken law is proposed, because the verses quoted do not describe any act of worship. The KJV’s “an image” for the Hebrew “the teraphim”, the KJV’s “idolatry” at 15:23, and Brenton’s Greek word at 19:13 are stated here as wording and are not proposed as separate findings. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “teraphim” finds Judges 17:5, 18:14, 18:17, 18:18, 18:20 and Hosea 3:4 only, so the English word does not lead to this passage; the Hebrew word was confirmed by script in the Westminster Leningrad text of 1 Samuel 19:13, 19:16 and 15:23, Genesis 31:19 and 31:34, Judges 17:5 and 2 Kings 23:24, and the Hebrew Bible was not searched for its other occurrences; 1 Samuel 19:8–18 was read in the KJV. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the image was or whose it was. No H, G or V is proposed. title: Samuel “told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book” — what did the book say?

original.summary: When Saul is made king, Samuel tells the people “the manner of the kingdom”, writes it in a book and lays it up “before the Lord”. Two chapters earlier Samuel has told them “the manner of the king”: what a king will take from them. Deuteronomy has a law for a king, with limits on him and a book he is to copy. The verses compared do not say what Samuel wrote, or whether it was either of these.
original.reasoning: The book is made at the founding of the kingdom and is laid up “before the Lord”, so it may bear on the terms of Israel’s kingship. The verse names its subject without reproducing its contents. The same Hebrew noun, mishpat, heads the speech of 8:11–17, where it introduces what a king will take; there the people are warned, and nothing is said of a writing. Deuteronomy 17:14–20 sets limits on a king and speaks of a book he is to copy, and the KJV of those verses does not use the phrase of 10:25. Whether Samuel’s book set out the king’s claims on the people, limits on the king, or something else decides how Saul’s later acts and Samuel’s rebukes of him are to be measured.

title: “Because he slew the Gibeonites” — when and how did Saul slay them?

original.summary: A three-year famine is said to be “for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites”, and seven of Saul’s descendants are put to death for it. The chapter says that Saul “sought to slay them” and that he “consumed” them, but the verses compared do not give the time, place, extent or circumstances of the killing; and a word search finds no Gibeonite named in 1 Samuel, the book that tells Saul’s reign.
original.reasoning: The chapter does state the charge and its ground. The Lord’s answer names the act (“he slew the Gibeonites”), 21:2 names the oath Israel had sworn and Saul’s motive (“in his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah”), and the Gibeonites describe a man who “consumed us” and planned that they should not remain “in any of the coasts of Israel”. The verses compared state that killing occurred but do not give its time in Saul’s reign, place, number killed or detailed circumstances; 21:1 says “slew”, while 21:2 says “sought to slay”. The charge is laid on “his bloody house” as well as on Saul, and no act of the house is told here. The gap matters to the passage, because a famine and the death of seven men, who are not said in these verses to have taken part, rest on an act that the chapter mentions only by reference.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the killing took place at Nob, the city of the priests smitten in Saul’s reign (1 Samuel 22:19), on the view that Gibeonites served there as the “hewers of wood and drawers of water … for the altar” of Joshua 9:27; that it is connected with the flight of the people of Beeroth, one of the four Gibeonite cities of Joshua 9:17, told at 2 Samuel 4:3; that it was an act of Saul’s reign that no book narrates. Limits: 1 Samuel 22:19 names priests and a city and does not name Gibeonites; 2 Samuel 4:3 gives no cause for the flight and does not name Saul; “slew” at 21:1 and “sought to slay” at 21:2 can both be true of one campaign that killed some and aimed at all, so they are not set against each other here; that the event is not told does not show that it did not happen; the Greek of 21:5 has the added words “and pursued us”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. title: “After forty years” — forty years counted from what, before Absalom asked to go to Hebron?

original.summary: Absalom’s request to go to Hebron, which opens his revolt, is dated “after forty years”. The verse does not say from what the forty years are counted. The time notes just before it are three years and two years, David’s whole reign is given as forty years, and Absalom is listed among the sons born to David in Hebron.
original.reasoning: The verse gives a number and no starting point. The periods the narrative has just named are short: three years at Geshur (13:38) and “two full years” in Jerusalem (14:28), followed by “after this” (15:1). The larger figures stated elsewhere do not supply an evident starting point either. David “reigned forty years” in all (5:4; 1 Kings 2:11), and at 15:7 he is still king, with the revolt and what follows it still to come. Absalom is listed among the sons born to David in Hebron (3:2–3), where David reigned seven years and six months (5:5); if he was born during that Hebron reign, forty years counted from his birth would reach the very end of David’s forty years or pass it. So the passage dates the opening of the revolt by a figure whose reference the verses compared leave unstated, and the order and length of the events of David’s reign depend on how it is taken.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the forty years run from an earlier event that the verse does not name, such as David’s anointing or the beginning of the kingdom; that the number was once a smaller one. Limits: both editions quoted have “forty” at 15:7, and no text with another number was examined in this session; the statement about Absalom’s birth rests on the condition that he was born while David reigned in Hebron, which 3:2–5 places there without giving a year; the chapters after 15 are not shown to stand in order of time, so the figure is not set here against the length of David’s reign as a contradiction; the vow of 15:8 is dated to the stay at Geshur, which 13:38 gives as three years, and that does not give the forty years a starting point. Brenton’s Greek of 15:7 has “to his father” where the KJV has “unto the king”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. title: Ziba or Mephibosheth — whose account of the day David fled was true?

original.summary: When David flees Jerusalem, Ziba tells him that Mephibosheth has stayed behind expecting to be given “the kingdom of my father”, and David gives Ziba all that was Mephibosheth’s. When David returns, Mephibosheth says “my servant deceived me” and that Ziba “hath slandered thy servant”. David answers, “Thou and Ziba divide the land.” The verses compared do not say which of the two accounts was true.
original.reasoning: The narrative reports two speeches that give opposite accounts of why Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem. Ziba says Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem because he expected the kingdom; Mephibosheth says he meant to ride to the king, that his servant deceived him, and that the servant slandered him. The narrator does add one statement in its own voice: Mephibosheth “had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace” (19:24). It does not say what that shows, and it does not say that Ziba lied or that Mephibosheth did. David’s answer, “Thou and Ziba divide the land”, neither restores the grant of chapter 9 nor confirms the grant of 16:4. Which account is true decides how both of David’s decisions are to be read: whether 16:4 took the land from a loyal man on a false report, and whether 19:29 is a judgment or a refusal to judge.

Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Ziba lied to obtain the land, for which the narrator’s statement at 19:24 is offered; that Mephibosheth did hope for the kingdom and Ziba reported it truly, for which his remaining in Jerusalem is offered; that David could not tell which was true and divided the land for that reason. Limits: 19:24 is the narrator’s statement about Mephibosheth’s appearance and is consistent with his account, but the passage draws no conclusion from it; Ziba’s words at 16:3 and Mephibosheth’s at 19:26–27 are speeches of the two men, not statements of the narrator; no reason is given for David’s decision at 19:29, and “I have said” there does not identify which earlier word is meant; Mephibosheth’s reply at 19:30 does not say whether the division was carried out. title: “again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel” — for what, before David numbered the people?

original.summary: The chapter opens with the Lord’s anger already kindled “against Israel”, before describing David being moved to number the people. Seventy thousand die. David says the sin is his and asks of the people, “these sheep, what have they done?” The verses compared name no act of Israel that the anger was for, and do not say to what earlier anger “again” looks back.
original.reasoning: In the order of 24:1 the anger comes first and the numbering second: the anger is “against Israel”, and David is moved “against them”. In that presentation, the numbering is not identified as the cause of the opening anger; the sentence’s order alone does not establish an independently dated sequence. The sin the chapter does name is David’s (“I have sinned greatly in that I have done”), and David himself separates the people from it (“these sheep, what have they done?”), yet it is the people who die. “Again” says that this anger follows an earlier one, and the verse does not name it. The parallel at 1 Chronicles 21:1 opens without any statement of anger, and 1 Chronicles 21:7 places God’s displeasure after the numbering, “with this thing”. So the verses compared leave unstated what Israel had done, and the answer bears on how the deaths of 24:15 are to be understood.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. title: “But he lied unto him” — why did the old prophet of Bethel lie to the man of God?

original.summary: An old prophet of Bethel tells the man of God from Judah that an angel has ordered him to bring him home to eat, and the narrator adds “But he lied unto him.” The man of God eats, is sentenced by the word of the Lord spoken through the same old prophet, and is killed by a lion. The verses read state the lie and its result; they do not state why the old prophet told it.
original.reasoning: The chapter states a good deal about the old prophet. His sons told him what the man of God had done and said (13:11); he rode after him and invited him home (13:15); when refused, he claimed an angel’s command, and the narrator says in the same verse that this was a lie (13:18). The word of the Lord then came to that same prophet at the table, and he spoke the sentence (13:20–22). After the death he said the man “was disobedient unto the word of the Lord” (13:26), buried him in his own grave, mourned “Alas, my brother!”, asked to be buried beside him, and affirmed that the saying against the altar “shall surely come to pass” (13:30–32). What none of these verses gives is the reason for the lie. The gap matters to the passage: the man of God had been charged to eat no bread there (13:9), he had refused the same invitation once (13:16–17), the lie is the stated means by which he was brought back, and his death follows from it.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the old prophet wished to test whether the man of God would keep his charge; that he wanted the company or the honour of a man whose word had just been confirmed by a sign; that he acted for Bethel and its altar, to undo or discredit the message; that he sought a tie with the man of God for his own sake, in the light of his later request to lie in the same grave. Limits: the narrator’s words fix that the claim of an angel was a lie and do not describe the speaker’s purpose; the chapter records no reproof of the old prophet in the verses read, and that is not evidence of how the act was judged; the sentence at 13:21–22 is addressed to the man of God and names his own disobedience as its ground. The Greek of 13:31 has the added words “that my bones may be preserved with his bones”: that states a purpose for the burial request, not for the lie, and 2 Kings 23:18 reports that both sets of bones were left alone. It is a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of the whole Bible; a passage that speaks of this man in other words would not be found by them. title: Elijah is told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha — did Elijah anoint any of them?

original.summary: At Horeb the Lord tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel and Elisha prophet in his place. In the verses read, Elijah casts his mantle on Elisha; it is Elisha who tells Hazael he will be king; and a young prophet sent by Elisha pours oil on Jehu. The verses read report no anointing done by Elijah, and they do not say how the command given to him was carried out.
original.reasoning: The command is in the second person and names three acts for Elijah: “anoint Hazael”, Jehu “shalt thou anoint”, Elisha “shalt thou anoint”. The verses read report something for each of the three men. Elijah finds Elisha and casts his mantle on him, and Elisha follows and serves him (19:19–21); the verse names a mantle and does not name oil or use the word “anoint”. With Hazael it is Elisha who speaks, at Damascus, and his words are that the Lord has shown him that Hazael will be king (2 Kings 8:13); no oil and no word “anoint” stands in 8:7–15. Jehu is anointed with oil, by “one of the children of the prophets” whom Elisha sends (2 Kings 9:1–6). The command lists Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, while the account presents Elisha, Hazael and Jehu. The list does not explicitly require that the acts occur in its stated order. The gap matters because the command is the Lord’s answer to Elijah at Horeb and sets out what is to follow; the verses read do not say whether Elijah did any of the three acts himself, or by what step the task passed to Elisha.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Elijah carried out the command through his successor, so that what Elisha did or ordered counts as done by Elijah; that “anoint” is used here for appointing or designating, so that the mantle and the spoken word answer to it; that Elijah did anoint one or more of the three in acts the books do not report; that the command was left in part undone by Elijah. Limits: the command sets no time and does not say that Elijah must act in person at each step; that an act is not reported does not show that it was not done; 2 Chronicles 22:7 says the Lord had anointed Jehu and names no human hand; the casting of the mantle is not called an anointing in the verses read, and it is not said there to be anything else. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of 1 and 2 Kings in full; an account that uses other words would not be found by them. title: Twelve pieces, ten tribes and “one tribe” — which tribe is the twelfth?

original.summary: Ahijah tears a garment into twelve pieces, gives Jeroboam ten for “ten tribes”, and says Solomon’s son shall have “one tribe”. Ten and one make eleven. In the KJV and the Hebrew, the verses read do not say whose the twelfth piece is or which tribe it stands for; Brenton’s Greek reads “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36.
original.reasoning: The sign gives the numbers itself: twelve pieces (11:30), ten to Jeroboam for “ten tribes” (11:31, 11:35), and “one tribe” for Solomon’s line (11:13, 11:32, 11:36). The prophet does not say what becomes of the two remaining pieces, and the sum of the tribes named is eleven. The account that follows says first that none followed the house of David “but the tribe of Judah only” (12:20) and in the next verse that Rehoboam gathered “all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin” (12:21). So in the KJV and the Hebrew quoted, the verses read leave open which tribe the twelfth piece stands for and on which side it is counted. The gap matters because the sign is the stated ground of the division of the kingdom, and the count is its content. The Greek quoted does give a count that reaches twelve at two of the verses: it has “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36 and “Judah and Benjamin” at 12:20, while at 11:13 it has “one tribe”, as the Hebrew does.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the KJV and Hebrew verses quoted state: that the twelfth tribe is Benjamin, held with Judah by Rehoboam (12:21, 12:23; 2 Chronicles 11:12), and that “one tribe” means one beside Judah, David’s own; that “one tribe” is Judah, with Benjamin or Simeon counted within it (Joshua 19:1 places Simeon’s inheritance inside Judah’s); that Levi, which had no territory of its own, is the tribe left out of the count; that “ten” and “one” are round figures for the greater part and the lesser. The Greek quoted states the count of two at 11:32 and 11:36; it does not name the two there, and it names Judah and Benjamin at 12:20. Limits: the sign does not say that every piece stands for one tribe on one side, though 11:31 ties ten pieces to ten tribes; a list of the twelve tribes is not given in these verses, and the Bible counts the tribes in more than one way, so which names make up the “ten” is not fixed by the verses read; 12:20 and 12:21 can both be true if Benjamin joined Rehoboam after the people made Jeroboam king, a step the text does not report; the Greek readings are wording differences stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. title: “The book of the acts of Solomon” — what was this book, and is it the source Chronicles names?

original.summary: For the rest of Solomon’s acts and his wisdom, 1 Kings sends the reader to “the book of the acts of Solomon”. A phrase search of the packaged KJV finds that title in this verse only. At the same point 2 Chronicles names three other writings. The verses read do not say who wrote the book, what it held beyond the words quoted, or whether it is the same as any of the three.
original.reasoning: The verse names the book by a title and says what is in it: “the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom”. That much is stated. The verses read do not say who wrote it, when, or where it was kept, and the account of Solomon closes by pointing to it for what the account itself leaves out. At the matching place 2 Chronicles 9:29 points instead to “the book of Nathan the prophet”, “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” and “the visions of Iddo the seer”. title: “There was great indignation against Israel” — whose indignation, and why did Israel depart?

original.summary: Israel, Judah and Edom are winning the war against Moab when the king of Moab offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall. The next sentence says “there was great indignation against Israel”, and the armies go home. The verses read do not say whose indignation it was, why it fell on Israel, or how it made the armies leave.

Then one verse reports the offering of the king’s son and, straight after it, “great indignation against Israel”, followed by the withdrawal. The sentence names no one who was indignant. It does not say that the offering caused the indignation, although it is told directly before it, and it does not say what the indignation did. The gap matters to the passage because it is the stated turning point of the campaign: the armies that were winning “departed from him, and returned to their own land”.

title: “The blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons” — what happened to Naboth's sons?

original.summary: When Jehu has Joram’s body thrown into Naboth’s field, he recalls a word of the Lord about “the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons”. The account of Naboth’s death in 1 Kings 21 reports that Naboth was stoned and does not mention any sons. The verses read do not say when, how or by whom Naboth’s sons were killed.
original.reasoning: 2 Kings 9:26 gives, as the Lord’s own words, that he had seen “the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons”. In 1 Kings 21 the verses read tell of one death: Naboth is accused, carried out of the city and stoned (21:13), the message to Jezebel is “Naboth is stoned, and is dead” (21:14), and Elijah’s charge to Ahab speaks of “the blood of Naboth” (21:19). A whole-word search of 1 Kings 21 in the packaged KJV for “son” or “sons” finds only 21:10, 21:22 and 21:29, and none of those is about Naboth’s children. So the later verse refers to bloodshed that the earlier account, in the verses read, does not report. The gap matters because the sons’ blood is part of the stated ground for what is done to Joram’s body, and because Ahab then goes down “to take possession” of the vineyard (21:16), which Naboth had called the inheritance of his fathers.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the sons were put to death with Naboth, at the same time, and 1 Kings 21 leaves it out; that they were killed afterwards so that no heir could claim the vineyard; that “the blood of his sons” speaks of the loss done to his descendants and not of a separate killing. Limits: no conflict between the two books is asserted, since an account that reports one death does not deny others; 2 Kings 9:26 does speak of the sons’ blood, so what is missing is any report of the event, not the fact of bloodshed; the words Jehu recalls are not found in those words in 1 Kings 21:19, and whether they are a second saying or another form of the same one is not settled by these verses; “yesterday” is quoted as printed and its reference is not fixed here. Brenton’s Greek of 9:26 has “him” where the KJV has “I will requite thee”; that wording was seen and not examined. title: “The Lord gave Israel a saviour” — who was the saviour?

original.summary: In the account of Jehoahaz the narrator says that “the Lord gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians”. The verse does not name him, and the same chapter says that Hazael oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz”. The verses read do not say who the saviour was or when he came.
original.reasoning: The KJV and the Hebrew of 13:5 speak of a person given to Israel, by whom Israel came out from under Syria. The verse stands inside the account of Jehoahaz, after his prayer (13:4), yet the chapter also says that the king of Syria left Jehoahaz almost no army (13:7) and that Hazael oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz” (13:22). Relief is then reported under two later kings: Jehoash took back the cities and beat Benhadad three times (13:25), and of Jeroboam the narrator says the Lord “saved them by the hand of Jeroboam” (14:27), with the verb that belongs to the noun at 13:5. None of the verses read says that either king is the saviour of 13:5, and the verse itself gives no name, people or office. The identity matters to the passage because it is the stated answer to the king’s prayer and the stated means of Israel’s release.

title: “I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord” — which book was it, and how had it gone out of knowledge?

original.summary: In Josiah’s eighteenth year the high priest says he has “found the book of the law in the house of the Lord”. The king hears it, rends his clothes and reforms Judah by it. The verses read call it the book of the law and the book of the covenant, and Chronicles calls it a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses; they do not say how much writing it held, where it had been, or how it came to be found at that time.
original.reasoning: The verses read say several things about the book. It was found in the house of the Lord by Hilkiah (22:8; 23:24). It is called “the book of the law” (22:8, 22:11), “the book of the covenant” (23:2) and “the book of this covenant” (23:21), and Chronicles calls it “a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses” (2 Chronicles 34:14). Its words told of wrath because “our fathers have not hearkened” (22:13), it was read aloud to the people at one gathering (23:2), and a passover was kept “as it is written” in it (23:21). What the verses do not give is its extent, the place in the house where it lay, how long it had been unread, or what led to its discovery and the king’s response. Deuteronomy 31:26 tells of “this book of the law” being put beside the ark, and 2 Kings 14:6 has the narrator cite “the book of the law of Moses” for an act of an earlier king; neither verse says what became of that book between then and Josiah. The gap matters because the whole reform of chapters 22 and 23 is said to rest on this book.

Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book was Deuteronomy or a part of it; that it was the whole of the five books of Moses; that it was the copy laid beside the ark, lost or hidden during earlier reigns; that it was a writing first made known at that time. title: “There came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet” — when was it written, and how did it reach Jehoram?

original.summary: Jehoram of Judah receives a writing from Elijah that condemns him for killing his brothers, an act Chronicles places after his father Jehoshaphat’s death. Kings tells of Elijah being taken up into heaven before it tells of a campaign in which Jehoshaphat is still alive. The verses do not say when the writing was made or who carried it.
original.reasoning: The writing speaks of the killing of Jehoram’s brothers as already done, and Chronicles tells that killing after Jehoshaphat’s death. Kings tells of Elijah’s going up in its second chapter, and in its third has Jehoshaphat alive and Elisha introduced as the man who “poured water on the hands of Elijah”. The timing affects how the event is read: the writing may have arrived during Elijah’s earthly life, or after his departure, including a writing composed beforehand and delivered later. The quoted verses do not settle these possibilities.
original.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the quoted verses state: that Elijah was still on earth, the order of telling in Kings not being the order of events; that Jehoram had begun to reign while his father lived, as 2 Kings 1:17 and 8:16 may suggest, and the killings fall in that time; that Elijah wrote beforehand and the writing was delivered later; that the writing came from Elijah after he had been taken up; that another man of the name is meant. What the verses do state is that a writing came, that it was from Elijah the prophet, and what it said. The words “poured water on the hands of Elijah” describe Elisha’s past service and do not by themselves say that Elijah was gone. original.summary: Necho of Egypt tells Josiah that God has commanded him to make haste and warns him not to meddle with God. original.summary: The elders’ answer reported in Tatnai’s letter says that Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God. title: The foundation of the temple: laid in the second year of the return, or on the day Haggai names in the second year of Darius?

original.summary: Ezra says the builders laid the foundation of the temple in the second year after the return, and that the work then stopped until the second year of Darius. Haggai, speaking on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in the second year of Darius, names that date and adds “even from the day that the foundation of the Lord’s temple was laid”, and looks back to the time “before a stone was laid upon a stone”.
original.reasoning: In Ezra the laying of the foundation falls in the second year of the coming to Jerusalem, in the days of Cyrus, and is celebrated as done; the stoppage that follows lasts until the second year of Darius. In the KJV of Haggai the words “even from the day that the foundation of the Lord’s temple was laid” can be read as describing the date in Darius’s second year, and the same speech speaks of a time before stone was laid on stone in the temple.
original.scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV follows the Hebrew quoted in both books. The clash rests on reading the last clause of Haggai 2:18 as naming the same day as the date before it, a reading suggested, but not required, by the KJV’s “even”. The Hebrew sets a second “from” before “the day”, and Brenton’s Greek joins the two with “and”, so the clause can also be read as a second, earlier starting point; on that reading there is no clash. The two can also stand if the foundation was laid in the days of Cyrus and laid or begun again when the work was taken up under Darius; no verse quoted reports a second laying. title: “Wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel” — or “wrote in peace to Mithradates”?

original.summary: The KJV names three men who wrote to Artaxerxes: Bishlam, Mithredath and Tabeel. Brenton’s Greek has no Bishlam: it says the letter was written “in peace”, puts the name Mithradates in the form of the one written to, and then says that “the tribute-gatherer” wrote to the king.
original.reasoning: In the KJV three named men and their companions are the writers and the king is the one written to. title: Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes between Cyrus and Darius — which kings are meant, and is the order of telling the order of events?

original.summary: Ezra 4 tells of opposition from the days of Cyrus “until the reign of Darius”, then of an accusation under Ahasuerus and letters under Artaxerxes about the city and its walls, and then says the work on the house stopped until the second year of Darius. The verses do not say who these two kings are or whether their reigns fall before Darius.
original.reasoning: The answer changes what the chapter reports. If the two kings reigned between Cyrus and Darius, the letters may be read as preceding and contributing to the stoppage of 4:24; sequence alone does not establish that causal link. If they are later kings, the chapter gathers opposition from several reigns and 4:24 takes up again from 4:5; the letters then concern a later building of the city, which is what they speak of: in the KJV of Ezra 4:8–23 the words “house” and “temple” do not occur, and the letters speak of the city and its walls. The book also names an Artaxerxes after Darius among those by whose commandment the house was finished, though it dates the finishing to Darius’s sixth year.

title: “Some of them had wives by whom they had children” — what became of the wives and the children?

original.summary: The book proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives “and such as are born of them”, reports an inquiry that finished on a stated day, records a pledge by the priests first named, lists the men, and ends by saying that some had children by these wives. Whether the families were in fact divided, and what happened to the women and children if they were, bears on how the whole episode is read. The verses quoted report the proposal, the congregation’s assent, the inquiry and its end, a pledge by the priests of verse 18, and a list of names; the putting away is reported as a pledge and an inquiry concluded, not described as an event.

title: Chisleu “in the twentieth year”, then Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes” — how is the year counted, and whose year is the first?

original.summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Nehemiah hears the report from Jerusalem in the month Chisleu “in the twentieth year” and speaks to the king in the month Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes”. Elsewhere the KJV calls Chisleu the ninth month and Nisan the first. The book does not say from what point its years are counted, or whose twentieth year 1:1 means.
original.reasoning: The story runs from Chisleu to Nisan, and both are put in a twentieth year. If the year number changed with the first month, Nisan, a Chisleu of the twentieth year would be followed by a Nisan of the twenty-first; if the events are in the order told and both twentieth years use the same reckoning, the year did not change between them. How the years are counted decides how long Nehemiah waited and when his twelve years as governor began, and the verses quoted do not state it. Verse 1:1 also names no king.
original.scope: Possible readings, none stated in the verses quoted: that the king’s years are counted from the day or season he began to reign, not from Nisan; that the year is counted from the autumn; that “the twentieth year” of 1:1 belongs to some other count than the king’s; or that one of the two figures has been miscopied. Hebrew and Greek have “twentieth” in both verses, as the KJV does. The month numbers are taken from Zechariah 7:1 and Esther 3:7; a whole-word search of the packaged KJV finds Chisleu only at Nehemiah 1:1 and Zechariah 7:1 and Nisan only at Nehemiah 2:1 and Esther 3:7. title: “But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence” — why not?

original.summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The king commands that all bow to Haman, and Mordecai does not. He is asked why and no answer of his is reported; the passage says only that “he had told them that he was a Jew”. Haman’s plan to destroy all the Jews follows from this refusal, and the KJV does not state its reason.
original.reasoning: Everything that follows in the book turns on this refusal, yet the KJV reports the question put to Mordecai and not his reply. The one clue, that he had told them he was a Jew, is given as the reason the servants informed Haman; it is not said to be the reason he would not bow. In the two other verses quoted, Abraham and David bow to men and the verses record no blame.

title: “I know that my redeemer liveth” — who is the redeemer Job means?

original.summary: Job says he knows that his redeemer lives and will stand upon the earth. The verse does not say who the redeemer is. In the same speech Job says the hand of God has touched him, and in the next verse that he will see God.
original.reasoning: The verse names the redeemer only by what he is to Job. The chapter gives two things that pull apart: God is the one whose hand has touched Job (19:21), and God is the one Job will see (19:26). Earlier Job has said that there is no daysman between him and God (9:33) and that he has a witness in heaven (16:19), and has wished that one might plead for a man with God (16:21). Whether the redeemer of 19:25 is God himself, the witness of 16:19, or someone else is not said. The answer decides whether Job here appeals to God against God’s own treatment of him, or to another.

title: Elihu speaks from chapter 32 to chapter 37 — why does the Lord’s verdict name Job and three friends and not him?

original.summary: Elihu is first named at Job 32:2, angry with Job and with the three friends, and speaks through chapter 37. When the Lord gives his verdict he names Eliphaz and his “two friends” and Job. The verses quoted do not say whether Elihu spoke rightly, or why he is not named.
original.reasoning: The narrator says Elihu was angry with both sides. Elihu is introduced as speaker at 32:6, 34:1 and 35:1 and again at 36:1, and a search of the packaged KJV of chapters 32–37 for a line that introduces a speaker (“answered … and said”, “spake … and said”, “proceeded, and said”) finds those four verses only. title: Behemoth and leviathan — what creatures does the Lord point Job to?

original.summary: The Lord’s speech from the whirlwind (40:6) sets two creatures before Job, behemoth and leviathan, and describes each at length. The KJV keeps both words as names. The verses quoted do not say what kind of creature either one is.
original.reasoning: The speech uses the two creatures to answer Job, so what they are bears on what the answer is. The description joins things said of a grazing animal and a creature of the water (grass, a river, a hook) with things that go beyond that (a flame from the mouth, heads in the plural in the psalm, a kingship over “all the children of pride”). If they are animals Job could see, the speech can be read as pointing to God’s rule over the made world; if they are creatures of another kind, it can be read as pointing to powers beyond ordinary animals. The text names them and does not say which.

title: “Thou shalt keep them, O Lord” — who or what is kept: the poor and needy, or the words of the Lord?

title: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living” — what book is this, and what is lost when a name is blotted out?

original.summary: Psalm 69:28 asks that “them” be blotted out of “the book of the living” and “not be written with the righteous”. The verses quoted do not say what the book is or what follows from a name being removed.

What is lost depends on what the book is: a record of who is alive, a list of the righteous, or a record of those whom God counts for life. The verses of the psalm name neither the keeper nor the book’s other contents, and do not say whether blotting out concerns this life or another.

title: “the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim … came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon” or “the fourth year of Jehoiakim … the first year of Nebuchadrezzar”?

original.summary: Daniel 1:1 has Nebuchadnezzar, “king of Babylon”, come against Jerusalem “in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim”. Jeremiah 25:1 says the fourth year of Jehoiakim “was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon”. Jeremiah 46:2 puts his smiting of Pharaohnecho in that fourth year.
original.reasoning: Daniel 1:1 names Nebuchadnezzar “king of Babylon” in the third year of Jehoiakim. Jeremiah 25:1 gives the fourth year of Jehoiakim as the first year of Nebuchadrezzar, and 46:2 gives that fourth year for the battle at Carchemish. Read as worded, the king is called king of Babylon one year before his first year. The two statements could both stand if the two books count the years of a reign by different methods, or if the title in Daniel 1:1 is the title used of him when the event is told; neither passage says how the years are counted.
original.scope: No tag is proposed: the record compares the wording of the KJV only, and does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek. It does not say that either book is mistaken, and it does not say that the siege of Daniel 1:1 and the battle of Jeremiah 46:2 are the same event. The spellings Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuchadrezzar are the KJV’s two spellings of the name and are not the point.

title: “though thou be little among the thousands of Judah” (Micah) or “art not the least among the princes of Juda” (Matthew)?

original.summary: The KJV of Micah 5:2 has Bethlehem “little among the thousands of Judah”. The KJV of Matthew 2:6 has Bethlehem “not the least among the princes of Juda”.
original.reasoning: Micah’s clause says Bethlehem is “little” (Hebrew צעיר, Greek ὀλιγοστός) “among the thousands of Judah”. title: “the lord commended the unjust steward” — which lord?

original.summary: Luke 16:8 says “the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely”. title: Fowl brought forth by the waters, or formed from the ground? The Hebrew of Genesis 1:20 does not say the waters bring them forth

original.summary: The KJV of Genesis 1:20 and Brenton’s Greek have the waters bring forth fowl, while Genesis 2:19 forms the fowl from the ground. The Hebrew of 1:20 has the waters swarm with living creatures and the fowl fly, as a separate clause.
original.reasoning: Read in the KJV, the waters bring forth the moving creature and the fowl in chapter 1, while chapter 2 forms the fowl from the ground. Brenton’s Greek of 1:20 has one verb, “let the waters bring forth”, governing both the creeping creatures and the flying birds, so the Greek reads as the KJV does. The Hebrew has a verb for the waters (they swarm) whose object is the swarm of living creatures, and then a separate clause in which the fowl themselves fly. On the Hebrew wording, chapter 1 does not say what the fowl came from, and 2:19 says they were formed from the ground. The conflict therefore exists in the KJV and the Greek, and is not clearly present in the Hebrew.
original.scope: This is a demonstrated difference in clause structure, not a difference between synonymous English words. It does not show that the Hebrew has no tension with chapter 2: it says the fowl fly above the earth, and 1:22 has the fowl multiply “in the earth”, and some readers take the fowl to be among the creatures the waters produce. Genesis 1:24 has the earth bring forth the land animals, which is consistent with 2:19 for the beasts. The Hebrew is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text, and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament); NETS is an English translation of the Septuagint and is paraphrased only to show how the Greek is read; its PDF was not downloaded for this verification. original.summary: The KJV has God gather the sea waters “as an heap”. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has ὡσεὶ ἀσκόν, “as in a wineskin”.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
A heap is a pile of water standing up, and a wineskin is a bag that holds it. The KJV has the former. The Greek has ὡσεὶ ἀσκὸν. The Hebrew has כַּ֭נֵּד in that slot, and the KJV reading follows it. The two English pictures differ: waters piled up against a limit, or waters held inside a container.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
A heap is a pile of the waters standing on one another. A skin bottle is a vessel that holds them. The Greek ἀσκός is the word for a leather bag or wineskin, and Brenton’s English prints “bottle”. The two texts give two pictures of how the sea is gathered, as a mound in the KJV and as the contents of a container in the Greek.
original.scope:
Preserved draft scope:
T applies at 33:7 and only to this noun; the Greek and the KJV agree on the rest of the verse (gathering the sea, storing the deeps). The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together; this record does not say what the Hebrew word means or that “heap” is wrong. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek.
