title: “Slay them not” (Psalm 59:11) — “Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be” (59:13)

original.summary: In one prayer the speaker asks that his enemies not be slain, lest his people forget, and two verses later asks that they be consumed so that they are no more.
original.reasoning: Verse 11 asks that the enemies not be killed, giving a reason (so that the people do not forget) and asking instead that they be scattered and brought down. Verse 13 asks that they be consumed in wrath until they are not. The Hebrew keeps the contrast: אַל־תַּהַרְגֵ֤ (do not kill them) and כַּלֵּ֥ה twice (finish, consume) with וְֽאֵ֫ינֵ֥מֹו (and they are not). The Greek has Μὴ ἀποκτείνῃς αὐτοὺς (do not kill them) and καὶ οὐ μὴ ὑπάρξουσι (and they shall not exist). The KJV and Hebrew juxtapose requests to spare and to consume. The Greek also juxtaposes not killing and destruction, but its destruction clause is not grammatically identical to the Hebrew imperatives. This does not establish inconsistent intentions.
original.scope: This sets two requests of one prayer beside each other in the KJV, the Hebrew and the Greek. It does not say the psalm contradicts itself or that the writer was inconsistent. The two verses may be read as two stages (scattering now, consuming later), or “not be” may mean their power or standing rather than their lives; the psalm does not say which. Both are the speaker’s prayers, not statements about what God does. The verses are poetry and the comparison is of the words printed. This record compares the requests in verses 11 and 13; it does not claim that the KJV, Hebrew and Greek agree in all details. Greek 58:12 has “your law” where Hebrew 59:12/KJV 59:11 has “my people”; the separate translation finding retains Brenton’s variant note. title: “Sore broken us in the place of dragons” — the Greek has “a place of affliction”

original.reasoning: Both texts name the place where the people were crushed or brought low. The KJV names it “the place of dragons”, a place where creatures live. A reader of the English pictures a lair of creatures; a reader of the Greek pictures a place of suffering.

title: “Save, Lord: let the king hear us when we call” — the Greek asks the Lord to save the king

original.summary: The KJV ends the psalm with a call to the Lord to save, and then asks that the king hear us. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, asks the Lord to save the king and to hear us; the king is the one saved, not the one who hears.
original.reasoning: In the KJV the king is the subject of the second clause: “let the king hear us when we call”. In the Greek the king is the object of the first clause, σῶσον τὸν βασιλέα, “save the king”, and the one who hears is the same Lord who is addressed: ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν, “hear us”. The two verses therefore name different people as the one who hears the prayer, and they give the king a different place in the line, as the one acted upon in the Greek and as the one who hears in the KJV.

The Hebrew has הַלְּבָנָה, “the white one”, the usual poetic word for the moon, and הַחַמָּה, “the hot one”, the sun. The Greek has the nouns for brick (πλίνθος) and wall (τεῖχος). title: “So shall he sprinkle many nations” — the Greek has “so shall many nations wonder at him”

The KJV makes the servant the actor who sprinkles the nations. In the Greek the nations are the actors who wonder at him. title: “That prepare a table for that troop … unto that number” — the Greek has “a table for the demon” and “a cup for Fortune”

original.summary: The KJV reproaches those who “prepare a table for that troop, and … furnish the drink offering unto that number”. Brenton’s Greek has ἐτοιμάζοντες τῷ δαιμονίῳ τράπεζαν, καὶ πληροῦντες τῇ τύχῃ κέρασμα — “preparing a table for the demon, and filling a cup for Fortune”.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew has לַגַּד and לַמְנִי (gad and meni). The KJV renders them as the common nouns “troop” and “number”. The Greek gives two powers to whom the table and the cup are offered: a δαιμόνιον and Τύχη, Fortune. A reader of the English meets a crowd and a count; a reader of the Greek meets two objects of worship.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The Hebrew has הַעֹרְכִים לַגַּד שֻׁלְחָן וְהַמְמַלְאִים לַמְנִי מִמְסָךְ, “those setting for Gad a table, and those filling for Meni a mixed [drink]”. The prefixed ל is a preposition; it does not by itself prove that the words are proper names. NET’s translator notes identify Gad and Meni as deity names and cite HALOT. The KJV renders them as “that troop” and “that number”, as common nouns, and not as names. The Greek has τῷ δαιμονίῳ, “to the demon”, and τῇ τύχῃ, “to fortune”, and treats the objects of the offering as divine or spiritual beings.

title: “He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man” — the Greek has “the transgressor that sacrifices a calf is as he that kills a dog”

original.summary: The KJV compares a worshipper’s sacrifice with a crime: “He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man; he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog’s neck.” Brenton’s Greek has Ὁ δὲ ἄνομος ὁ θύων μοι μόσχον, ὡς ὁ ἀποκτέννων κύνα — “The lawless one who sacrifices a calf to me is as one who kills a dog” — with a single transgressor and one pair of acts.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The KJV has four pairs of offering and offence (ox and man, lamb and dog’s neck, oblation and swine’s blood, incense and blessing an idol). The Greek has three (calf and dog, fine flour and swine’s blood, frankincense and blasphemy). It names the sacrificer ἄνομος, “lawless”, which the KJV does not. The offerings are also not the same: ox against calf, and the lamb pair is not in the Greek.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The Hebrew has שׁוֹחֵט הַשּׁוֹר מַכֵּה־אִישׁ, “one slaughtering the ox, one striking a man”, then זוֹבֵחַ הַשֶּׂה עֹרֵף כֶּלֶב, “one sacrificing the lamb, one breaking a dog’s neck”. The Greek has a single clause for the offering of a calf: ὁ θύων μοι μόσχον, ὡς ὁ ἀποκτέννων κύνα, “the one sacrificing a calf to me, as one killing a dog”. The man-slaying comparison is not there, and the offerer is called ἄνομος, “lawless”. The last comparison also differs: the KJV has “as if he blessed an idol” (מְבָרֵךְ אָוֶן); the Greek has ὡς βλάσφημος, “as a blasphemer”.

title: “Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow” — the Greek has “Phud, and Lud, and Mosoch”

original.summary: In the KJV the escaped are sent “to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow, to Tubal, and Javan”. Brenton’s Greek has εἰς Θαρσίς, καὶ Φούδ, καὶ Λούδ, καὶ Μοσόχ, καὶ εἰς Θοβέλ, καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα — “to Tarsis, and Phud, and Lud, and Mosoch, and to Thobel, and to Greece”.

Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew has פּוּל וְלוּד מֹשְׁכֵי קֶשֶׁת, which the KJV reads as Pul and Lud, “that draw the bow” (a description). The Greek reads the participle as a place or people name, Mosoch (Meshech), so that the list has an extra nation in place of the description. title: “Him that waiteth for him” (Isaiah) — “them that love him” (1 Corinthians): the quoted line is not worded the same

original.summary: 1 Corinthians 2:9 introduces its words with “as it is written” and says eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither entered into the heart of man the things God hath prepared for them that love him. The nearest verse in the KJV, Isaiah 64:4, says men have not heard nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him. The wording differs in the persons, the order and the content.
original.reasoning: Isaiah’s verse is addressed to God: the eye has not seen “a god beside you” who acts for the one who waits (לִמְחַכֵּה־לוֹ). Paul’s sentence is about what God prepared for those who love him (τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν). The two differ in the object (him that waiteth against them that love), in the order (ear then eye against eye then ear), and in the clause “neither have entered into the heart of man”, which the KJV Isaiah 64:4 does not have. The Hebrew has no verb for “entered into the heart”.
original.scope: This is a direct wording contrast between a passage and a later quotation of it, KJV against KJV, with the Hebrew and the Greek New Testament beside it. It is untagged: the record does not claim a mistranslation. It does not say Paul quotes Isaiah 64:4 alone; other passages (such as Isaiah 65:17) have been proposed as sources and the record does not decide between them. original.summary: The KJV says Jeroboam ordained priests for the high places, “for the devils” and for the calves. Preserved draft reasoning:
The KJV names the second class served by the priests as “devils”, which are beings. The Hebrew word is הַשְּׂעִירִים, the plural noun that Leviticus 16:8 prints for the two goats and that the published Leviticus 17:7 record already sets beside the KJV’s “devils”. Brenton’s Greek here uses two plural nouns, “the idols” and “the vain things”, and does not call them devils. The Hebrew has one word where the Greek has two.

The Greek has two Greek nouns in that place, εἰδώλοις (idols) and ματαίοις (vain things). Neither text prints a word for evil spirits.

title: Jehoiada’s coup: “let none come into the house of the Lord, save the priests” — or captains and the guard brought in?

original.summary: In 2 Chronicles 23 Jehoiada orders that none enter the house of the Lord except priests and ministering Levites, and the Levites guard the king. In 2 Kings 11 he brings the captains and the guard to himself in the house of the Lord, swears them there, and sets two parts of them to keep its watch.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The two accounts of the same coup describe the force differently. Chronicles names the third entering on the sabbath as “of the priests and of the Levites”, gatekeepers of the thresholds, forbids anyone else to enter the house of the Lord, and has the Levites compass the king. Kings names the men as the commanders of hundreds with the Carites and the runners (KJV “captains and the guard”), brings them into the house of the Lord, swears them there, assigns a third to the king’s house, and sets “two parts” to keep the watch of the house of the Lord about the king. The gates also differ in name: Kings has “the gate of Sur” and “the gate behind the guard”; Chronicles has “the gate of the foundation” (Brenton: “the middle gate”). One account has only temple personnel inside the house; the other has the armed guard inside it.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
Both passages divide the incoming sabbath watch into thirds. In Chronicles the thirds are porters of the doors (priests and Levites), the king’s house, and the gate of the foundation, and the Levites compass the king. In Kings the thirds are the king’s house, the gate of Sur, and the gate behind the guard, two parts keep the watch of the Lord’s house, and the addressed company compass the king. The first account names priests and Levites as the watch; the second names captains and the guard.
original.scope:
Preserved draft scope:
Untagged: the KJV, the Hebrew and the Greek agree with each other in each book, and the difference is between the two books. The two can be read together, since 2 Chronicles 23:1 names five captains of hundreds and 23:8 has “the Levites and all Judah” carry out the plan, so the men may have been the same people described in different terms, or the guard may have been posted outside the house. Neither text says so. The record sets the two wordings side by side and does not say either is in error. title: Uzziah’s burial: “in the field of the burial which belonged to the kings” — or “in the city of David”?

original.summary: 2 Chronicles says the leprous king was buried with his fathers “in the field of the burial which belonged to the kings”. 2 Kings says Azariah was buried with his fathers “in the city of David”. Both name Jotham as the successor.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
Both verses report the burial of the king who was succeeded by Jotham and who was buried “with his fathers”. Kings gives the place as the city of David. Chronicles gives it as a field of burial belonging to the kings, and adds the reason, that he was a leper. The Hebrew and the Greek read as the KJV does in both books. 2 Kings 15:1 calls the king Azariah and 2 Chronicles 26:1 calls him Uzziah; the two chapters give the same reign length (fifty-two years) and the same successor.

Both verses say the burial was with his fathers. Chronicles gives the place as a field of the burial belonging to the kings, with the reason that he was leprous. Kings gives the city of David. The two places are named differently.

title: Solomon’s merchants received “linen yarn” — the Greek of 2 Chronicles has no yarn

original.summary: The KJV says the king’s merchants received “linen yarn” at a price. The Hebrew prints one word, מִקְוֵא, twice, and Brenton’s Greek of 2 Chronicles 1:16 names no goods at all. Brenton’s Greek of 1 Kings 10:28 reads the same place as “from Thekoue”.
original.reasoning: In the KJV the second item bought in Egypt beside horses is “linen yarn”, a commodity. The Hebrew has the word מִקְוֵא (2 Chronicles) or מִקְוֵה (1 Kings) in the same slot, twice in each verse. Brenton’s Greek of 2 Chronicles 1:16 has no word for goods there: the traders’ “price” and “going” appear, and nothing is said to be received. Brenton’s Greek of 1 Kings 10:28 has the name Θεκουέ, a place from which the merchants came. The Greek therefore gives either no goods (Chronicles) or a place (Kings) where the KJV has a commodity.

original.summary: The KJV says the Lord smote the men of Bethshemesh “because they had looked into the ark of the Lord”. The Hebrew says כִּי רָאוּ בַּאֲרוֹן יְהוָה, “because they saw into the ark of the LORD”. Brenton’s Greek opens with a different clause: οὐκ ἠσμένισαν οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰεχονίου ἐν τοῖς ἀνδράσι Βαιθσαμύς, “the sons of Jechonias were not pleased with the men of Bethshemesh”, and then adds “because they saw the ark of the Lord”.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
In the Hebrew the cause of the slaughter is given in a single clause. In the Greek there is an additional group, the sons of Jechonias, who are displeased with the Bethshemesh men for seeing the ark, and the plague falls “among them”. A reader of the Greek has a named family in the story whom the Hebrew does not name. The number is the same in both: seventy men and fifty thousand men.

The Hebrew edition quoted prints a verb of smiting with the men of Beth-shemesh as object, followed by “because they saw the ark of the Lord”. The Greek printed at the same verse has the sons of Jeconiah as subject of a verb that is not smiting, and the smiting comes in a later clause. The KJV follows the Hebrew; the Greek prints a different first clause.

original.reasoning: The Hebrew edition quoted opens with a question, הֲלֹא־שָׁמַעְתָּ, “have you not heard”, and says the Lord made it from far-off days and formed it. The Greek printed at the same verse has two verbs spoken by the Lord, formed and gathered, and no question, no “heard” and no “long ago”. The KJV text asks the king whether he has heard; the Greek states what the Lord did.

The record does not compare the second half of the verse, where the sentence about fortified cities reads differently in the two texts, and does not claim the Hebrew and the Greek are two forms of the same sentence. title: “A conspiracy of her prophets” — the Brenton Greek says her princes

original.summary: The KJV says “There is a conspiracy of her prophets in the midst thereof, like a roaring lion”. The Hebrew prints קֶשֶׁר נְבִיאֶיהָ, “conspiracy of her prophets”. Brenton’s Greek prints οἱ ἀφηγούμενοι, “those who lead”, which Brenton’s English renders “princes”.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew subject is a conspiracy belonging to her prophets (נְבִיאֶיהָ), the KJV’s word. The Brenton Greek has a plural participle meaning leaders or rulers, and has no word for prophets or for a conspiracy; its first clause begins with the relative “whose”. The prophets are then named again in the next verses (22:28), so both texts mention prophets in the passage, but not in this clause.

title: “Ye eat with the blood … ye stand upon your sword” — the Brenton Greek page does not print these clauses

original.summary: The KJV has two charges against those left in the waste places: eating with the blood and lifting eyes to idols (33:25) and standing on the sword, working abomination and defiling a neighbour’s wife (33:26). The Hebrew prints both verses in full. Brenton’s Greek page ends verse 25 after “therefore say to them, Thus saith the Lord God” and prints no verse 26; its next verse, 27, begins at “As I live”.

Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew of 33:25 and 33:26 both close with “and shall ye possess the land?” (וְהָאָרֶץ תִּירָשׁוּ). The Brenton Greek page does not print either of those charges or the question, and the Greek numbering has 32 verses where the Hebrew and KJV have 33. Verses 27 onward align by number (KJV 27 = Greek 27).

title: “The east country … the desert” — the Brenton Greek prints Galilee and Arabia

original.summary: The KJV says the waters “issue out toward the east country, and go down into the desert”. The Hebrew prints אֶל־הַגְּלִילָה הַקַּדְמוֹנָה … עַל־הָעֲרָבָה, “to the district (Galilah) eastward … upon the Arabah”. Brenton’s Greek prints τὴν Γαλιλαίαν τὴν πρὸς ἀνατολάς … τὴν Ἀραβίαν, “Galilee that lies eastward … Arabia”.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The KJV puts ordinary words, “east country” and “desert”, where the Greek prints the place names Galilee and Arabia. A reader of the KJV does not see either name; a reader of the Greek sees both.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The Hebrew edition quoted has אֶל־הַגְּלִילָה הַקַּדְמוֹנָה, “to the eastern region” (גְּלִילָה, a district or circuit, from the same root as the name Galilee), and עַל־הָעֲרָבָה, “down to the Arabah”, the rift valley or steppe. The KJV renders both as common nouns, “east country” and “desert”. The Greek printed at the same verse renders both as place names, Galilee and Arabia, so the two texts present the waters as flowing toward named regions and the KJV as flowing toward unnamed ones.

title: Ezekiel bears his baggage “upon thy shoulders” — the Brenton Greek has him lifted up on others’ shoulders

original.summary: In the sign of the exile the KJV has Ezekiel carry his baggage on his own shoulder through the hole in the wall (12:6, 12:7). The Hebrew prints עַל־כָּתֵף תִּשָּׂא, “on a shoulder you shall carry”, and עַל־כָּתֵף נָשָׂאתִי, “on a shoulder I carried”. Brenton’s Greek prints ἐπʼ ὤμων ἀναληφθήσῃ, “thou shalt be taken up on shoulders”, and ἐπʼ ὤμων ἀνελήφθην, “I was taken up on shoulders”.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew verbs are active: you carry, I carried. The Greek verbs are passive: you will be taken up, I was taken up. Brenton’s English renders the Greek with “on men’s shoulders” and has the prophet lifted. In the KJV the prophet carries the stuff; in the Greek he is carried.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The Hebrew edition quoted has בָּעֲלָטָה הוֹצֵאתִי עַל־כָּתֵף נָשָׂאתִי, “in the dark I brought out, on the shoulder I bore”, with Ezekiel as the one who carries. The Greek printed at the same verse has the passive ἀνελήφθην, so the shoulders on which he is lifted are not stated to be his own and the carrying is not said to be done by him. The KJV has him carry.

original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
In the KJV and the Hebrew the four winds picture the exiles being scattered; the call is to flee Babylon because the LORD has already scattered them. title: “My servant the BRANCH” in the Hebrew — “my servant Anatole” (the East, or Rising) in the Greek

original.summary:
The KJV prints “my servant the BRANCH” for the Hebrew צֶמַח. Brenton’s Greek prints Ἀνατολήν, “rising” or “the East”, and Brenton’s English margin points to Luke 1:78.

Additional retained draft evidence/qualification:
The KJV says Joshua’s fellows are men wondered at. The Hebrew is אַנְשֵׁי מוֹפֵת, “men of a sign”. Brenton’s Greek is ἄνδρες τερατοσκόποι, which Brenton renders “diviners”.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew word names a shoot or sprout. The Greek word Ἀνατολή means a rising (of the sun or a star) and the East. Brenton’s English margin at this verse points to Luke 1:78. A reader can therefore set the KJV’s plant image beside the Greek’s rising image for the same servant.

Additional retained draft evidence/qualification:
The Hebrew word מוֹפֵת means a sign or wonder (the KJV margin has “of wonder, or, sign”). The Greek compound τερατοσκόποι is built from “portent” and “watch”, and Brenton’s English renders it “diviners”. A reader of the KJV has companions who are themselves a sign; a reader of the Greek has companions who watch portents.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The Hebrew edition quoted has עַבְדִּי צֶמַח, “my servant Tsemach”, the word the KJV prints as BRANCH, from the sense of something that sprouts. The Greek printed has Ἀνατολήν, which is the ordinary Greek word for a rising and for the east. The KJV puts a growth image in the verse; the Greek puts a rising image. Both translators treat the word as a title or name.

title: The stone with seven eyes — “I will engrave the graving thereof” in the Hebrew, “I am digging a trench” in the Greek

original.summary: The KJV has the LORD engrave an engraving on the stone. The Hebrew is מְפַתֵּחַ פִּתֻּחָהּ. Brenton’s Greek is ὀρύσσω βόθρον, “I am digging a pit”, and goes on to say the LORD “will search out” the iniquity of the land.
original.reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
In the Hebrew the LORD cuts an inscription on the stone that has seven eyes. In the Greek he digs a pit and then probes the land’s iniquity. The two images are different: carving a stone against digging the ground. The following clause also differs (“remove” against “search out”): the KJV has the LORD take the iniquity away, the Greek has him examine it.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The Hebrew edition quoted has הִנְנִי מְפַתֵּחַ פִּתֻּחָהּ, “behold I am engraving its engraving”, and וּמַשְׁתִּי אֶת־עֲוֹן הָאָרֶץ, “I will remove (or remove the guilt of) the iniquity of the land”. The KJV has the stone being engraved and the guilt taken away; the Greek has a pit dug and the unrighteousness searched out.
